# Abstract {-}

A probability model can perform well during internal validation yet behave differently when the population in which it is deployed differs from the population in which it was developed. This study investigates that problem through a unified empirical and simulation analysis of loan-default prediction. The empirical component uses 255,347 loan records with 29,653 recorded defaults (approximately 11.6%) to establish a probability model, assess calibration, and select an operating threshold. Logistic regression, ridge logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting are compared using validation log loss as the primary probability-quality criterion. Raw logistic regression achieved the lowest validation log loss and, on the locked test set, achieved ROC-AUC 0.7585, PR-AUC 0.3288, Brier score 0.09085, and log loss 0.31111. A validation-selected balanced-accuracy threshold of 0.1175 produced held-out recall of 68.4% and specificity of 70.1%.

The central research question is whether those statistical properties remain stable when the deployment distribution changes. Because the empirical data do not contain documented temporal cohorts or an independent deployment population, controlled Monte Carlo experiments are used to isolate covariate shift, intercept changes in the conditional outcome mechanism, and changes in predictor effects. Across 500 replications per condition, pure covariate shift produced little excess probability error when the conditional logistic model was correctly specified, whereas covariate shift combined with omitted nonlinear structure produced substantial calibration and probability deterioration. Under intercept outcome shift, calibration changed markedly while model ranking remained close to the oracle. Under slope outcome shift, the original model's ROC-AUC declined from approximately 0.762 to 0.473 as the predictor--outcome relationship reversed, while the oracle remained informative. Decision-threshold experiments also showed that the balanced-accuracy-optimal threshold can change substantially after population shift even when the conditional probability model remains correctly specified.

The results show that discrimination, calibration, probability accuracy, and decision-threshold stability are distinct properties of a predictive system. Internal predictive performance should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of deployment stability without temporal or external validation. Because the recorded `Default` label has no documented observation horizon, the empirical estimates are interpreted as risk of the recorded outcome rather than formal 12-month or lifetime probabilities of default.

**Keywords:** loan default; distribution shift; covariate shift; logistic regression; probability calibration; model misspecification; decision threshold; Monte Carlo simulation

\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Introduction

Loan-default prediction is fundamentally a problem of statistical prediction under uncertainty. A fitted model estimates the probability that a borrower experiences a recorded default outcome,

\[
p_i=P(Y_i=1\mid X_i),
\]

and a later decision rule may convert the estimated probability \(\widehat p_i\) into an operational action. The statistical validity of that system therefore depends on more than whether the model can classify observations correctly. The estimated probabilities should be appropriately calibrated, the model should rank higher-risk observations above lower-risk observations, and the operating threshold should remain appropriate for the population in which the model is used.

These properties are usually evaluated using held-out observations drawn from the same underlying source as the development data. That design is useful for internal validation but leaves an important question unresolved: **what happens when the deployment population no longer follows the same distribution as the development population?** Changes in borrower characteristics, underwriting practices, macroeconomic conditions, product mix, or the relationship between predictors and default can alter the statistical environment in which a model operates.

This distinction can be written formally. Let \(P(X,Y)\) denote the development joint distribution and \(Q(X,Y)\) the deployment joint distribution. Distribution shift occurs when

\[
P(X,Y)\neq Q(X,Y).
\]

The consequences depend on which part of the joint distribution changes. Under covariate shift,

\[
P(X)\neq Q(X),
\qquad
P(Y\mid X)=Q(Y\mid X),
\]

whereas a change in the conditional outcome mechanism occurs when

\[
P(Y\mid X)\neq Q(Y\mid X).
\]

These mechanisms need not affect a predictive model in the same way. A model may preserve ranking while losing calibration, remain probabilistically accurate while its operating threshold changes, or lose discrimination when predictor--outcome relationships themselves change.

The loan-default application in this paper provides an empirical baseline for studying these questions. The dataset contains a minority default outcome, making overall accuracy alone unsuitable for model assessment. Candidate probability models are compared using validation log loss, the selected model is assessed for discrimination and calibration, and a review threshold is selected independently using balanced accuracy. The empirical analysis therefore establishes the predictive system whose components are of interest: probability estimation, calibration, ranking, and threshold-based decision performance.

The empirical data, however, contain no documented temporal cohorts or genuinely independent deployment population. They cannot directly reveal how those components would respond to future population change. Controlled Monte Carlo simulation is therefore used as the second methodological component of the same study. The simulations hold some parts of the data-generating process fixed while deliberately changing others, allowing the effects of different forms of distribution shift to be isolated.

The study addresses five related questions:

1. **What level of internal probability performance, discrimination, and calibration is achieved by the empirical loan-default model selected under a prespecified validation criterion?**
2. **Under covariate shift, when does a fitted probability model remain stable, and when does model misspecification become increasingly consequential?**
3. **Can discrimination remain stable or improve while probability calibration deteriorates?**
4. **How does changing a predictor--outcome relationship affect discrimination and calibration when event prevalence is held approximately constant?**
5. **Can a decision threshold selected in the development population become inappropriate after population shift even when the underlying probability model remains useful?**

The contribution is not a claim that one algorithm is universally superior for credit risk, nor is the simulation intended to establish that a particular form of shift has occurred in the observed loan data. Instead, the paper uses a real prediction problem and controlled statistical experiments to study a broader question: **which properties of a probability-based predictive system remain stable under distributional change, and which must be reassessed?**

\clearpage

# Literature Review and Statistical Background

## Traditional and machine-learning credit scoring

Logistic regression remains a natural benchmark for binary credit outcomes because it models a conditional probability through the log-odds scale and produces interpretable coefficients. At the same time, contemporary credit-scoring research increasingly evaluates random forests, boosting, neural networks, and hybrid approaches that can represent nonlinear effects and higher-order interactions. Montevechi et al. (2024) review machine learning in consumer credit-risk modelling and emphasize both its potential and the need for standardized modelling procedures and interpretability. Ayari, Guetari, and Kraïem (2026), reviewing recent financial credit-scoring research, similarly identify predictive performance, dimensionality, interpretability, bias, and deployment complexity as recurring issues.

The existence of more flexible algorithms does not imply that they must outperform logistic regression in every dataset. Bazzana, Bee, and Hussin Adam Khatir (2024), for example, report that machine-learning methods produced only modest gains over logistic regression in their default-prediction application and argue that these gains must be weighed against implementation and interpretation costs. That observation motivates the validation-based comparison used here: complexity is treated as a candidate capability, not as evidence of superiority.

## Class imbalance and threshold selection

In an imbalanced credit portfolio, a 0.50 cutoff is not automatically appropriate. Bazzana, Bee, and Hussin Adam Khatir (2024) explicitly discuss threshold adjustment for default prediction because sensitivity and specificity cannot generally be maximized simultaneously. The statistical-learning principles make the same conceptual point more generally: fitting the conditional probability and choosing the final classification threshold are separate operations, and a different threshold can be justified when the consequences of the two types of classification error differ.

This paper uses balanced accuracy as the default threshold objective because verified monetary costs of false negatives and false positives are not available. Balanced accuracy gives equal weight to sensitivity and specificity. It is therefore a statistical operating objective, not a claim of economic optimality. The analysis also reports alternative validation-selected thresholds for F1, F2, and Youden's \(J\) so that the consequences of changing the objective are visible.

## Probability quality, calibration, and discrimination

Binary risk models should be evaluated along more than one dimension. Steyerberg et al. (2010) emphasize that discrimination, calibration, and overall predictive performance answer different questions. ROC-AUC measures ranking ability across thresholds, while precision-recall performance is especially informative when the positive class is less common. The Brier score summarizes squared probability error, and log loss penalizes probability assignments through the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood.

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities correspond to observed frequencies. Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) showed that different learning algorithms can produce systematically distorted probability scales and studied post-hoc methods including Platt scaling. Accordingly, this study does not assume that calibration must improve a model; raw and Platt-calibrated probabilities are compared on held-out validation data.


## Distribution shift and predictive stability

Internal validation estimates performance under the observed development environment. Deployment can violate that environment when the joint distribution of predictors and outcomes changes. Under covariate shift, the marginal predictor distribution changes while the conditional outcome mechanism remains invariant. In principle, a correctly specified conditional model can remain valid under such a shift because \(P(Y\mid X)\) is unchanged. Under misspecification, however, the approximation learned in the development population can become less accurate when deployment places more probability mass in regions where the approximation is poor (Shimodaira, 2000; Quiñonero-Candela et al., 2009; Wen, Yu, and Greiner, 2014).

A change in \(P(Y\mid X)\) represents a different problem. An intercept change in a logistic outcome mechanism can alter absolute risk while preserving much of the ranking induced by the original linear predictor. A change in predictor slopes can alter the ranking itself. These distinctions motivate separate assessment of discrimination, calibration, probability loss, and threshold performance rather than relying on a single metric such as ROC-AUC.

## Fairness, interpretability, and responsible use

Credit scoring is a high-consequence application in which predictive performance is not the only consideration. Kozodoi, Jacob, and Lessmann (2022) show that fairness criteria can interact with profitability and model design, while Das, Stanton, and Wallace (2023) review algorithmic fairness with particular attention to credit scoring. These studies motivate the subgroup diagnostics reported later in this paper. The available dataset does not contain the full set of attributes needed for a complete fairness audit, so the subgroup analysis is descriptive and should not be interpreted as establishing that the model is fair.


\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Statistical and Computational Framework

The analysis treats a predictive system as a sequence of connected but distinct statistical components:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Probability model}
\rightarrow
\text{Calibration}
\rightarrow
\text{Ranking}
\rightarrow
\text{Decision threshold}
\rightarrow
\text{Deployment stability}
}
\]

The empirical analysis estimates and evaluates the first four components under internal validation. The simulation analysis then studies the fifth component by changing the deployment data-generating mechanism while monitoring the same probability, calibration, ranking, and threshold quantities.

The statistical organization follows the factorization

\[
P(X,Y)=P(Y\mid X)P(X).
\]

This decomposition separates changes in the population of predictors from changes in the conditional outcome mechanism. The simulation experiments are therefore not separate applications: they are controlled perturbations of the same joint distribution underlying the empirical prediction problem. Covariate shift changes \(P(X)\) while holding \(P(Y\mid X)\) fixed; the outcome-shift experiments change \(P(Y\mid X)\). For each perturbation, the analysis asks how four observable properties respond:

\[
\boxed{
\text{probability accuracy},\quad
\text{calibration},\quad
\text{discrimination},\quad
\text{decision-rule stability}.
}
\]


The analysis is organized around the progression

\[
\text{statistical question}
\longrightarrow
\text{representation}
\longrightarrow
\text{model}
\longrightarrow
\text{objective/loss}
\longrightarrow
\text{computation}
\longrightarrow
\text{validation}
\longrightarrow
\text{decision}.
\]

Five principles guide the implementation:

1. **Representation matters.** Raw predictors must be converted into a numerical representation appropriate to the model.
2. **Loss defines the optimization target.** Logistic regression maximizes Bernoulli likelihood, while validation log loss evaluates probability quality on observations not used to estimate the model.
3. **Computation should be stable and reproducible.** Scaling and training-only preprocessing are used to avoid unnecessary numerical and leakage problems.
4. **Flexible models require validation.** Additional complexity is retained only when it improves held-out evidence.
5. **Probability fitting and classification are separate.** The threshold is optimized only after the probability model has been selected.

Decision objectives are evaluated over a grid and visualized so that the resulting trade-offs remain transparent.

# Data

```{r read-data}
loans <- read.csv(
  params$data_path,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

required_columns <- c(
  "LoanID","Age","Income","LoanAmount","CreditScore","MonthsEmployed",
  "NumCreditLines","InterestRate","LoanTerm","DTIRatio","Education",
  "EmploymentType","MaritalStatus","HasMortgage","HasDependents",
  "LoanPurpose","HasCoSigner","Default"
)

missing_columns <- setdiff(required_columns, names(loans))

if (length(missing_columns)) {
  stop("Missing columns: ", paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "))
}

if (anyNA(loans$LoanID) || anyDuplicated(loans$LoanID)) {
  stop("LoanID must be complete and unique.")
}

loans$Default <- as.integer(loans$Default)

if (anyNA(loans$Default) || !all(loans$Default %in% c(0,1))) {
  stop("Default must be coded 0/1 with no missing values.")
}

overview <- data.frame(
  Loans = nrow(loans),
  Predictors = length(required_columns) - 2,
  Defaults = sum(loans$Default),
  DefaultRate = mean(loans$Default),
  MissingCells = sum(is.na(loans))
)

overview_display <- overview
overview_display$DefaultRate <- sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * overview_display$DefaultRate)

paper_kable(
  overview_display,
  caption = "Dataset overview."
)
```

`LoanID` is an identifier and is not used as a predictor.

The study data are tabular loan-level observations. There is no observed repayment sequence, default date, recovery history, or time-varying balance. Therefore, recurrent or sequence models are not appropriate representations of the information available here.

```{r class-balance}
class_df <- data.frame(
  Outcome = c("Non-default","Default"),
  Count = c(sum(loans$Default == 0), sum(loans$Default == 1))
)

ggplot(class_df, aes(x = Outcome, y = Count)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  labs(
    title = "Observed Class Balance",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of loans"
  )
```

Because default is the minority outcome, raw accuracy can be misleading. Probability loss, ranking metrics, calibration, recall, precision, specificity, and review rate are examined instead.

## Predictor Construction

```{r predictor-setup}
numeric_features <- c(
  "Age","Income","LoanAmount","CreditScore","MonthsEmployed",
  "NumCreditLines","InterestRate","LoanTerm","DTIRatio"
)

categorical_features <- c(
  "Education","EmploymentType","MaritalStatus","HasMortgage",
  "HasDependents","LoanPurpose","HasCoSigner"
)

base_features <- c(numeric_features, categorical_features)

prepare_inputs <- function(d, include_age = TRUE) {
  x <- d[, base_features, drop = FALSE]

  for (nm in numeric_features) {
    x[[nm]] <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(x[[nm]])))
  }

  for (nm in categorical_features) {
    x[[nm]] <- trimws(as.character(x[[nm]]))
    x[[nm]][x[[nm]] == ""] <- NA_character_
  }

  x$LoanToAnnualIncome <- ifelse(
    is.finite(x$Income) & x$Income > 0,
    x$LoanAmount / x$Income,
    NA_real_
  )

  if (!include_age) {
    x$Age <- NULL
  }

  x
}

X_raw <- prepare_inputs(loans)
y <- loans$Default
```

The engineered ratio

\[
\text{LoanToAnnualIncome}
=
\frac{\text{LoanAmount}}{\text{Income}}
\]

captures loan size relative to annual income. It is derived only from variables already present in the data.

# Methods

## Development Design

The analysis uses four non-overlapping partitions:

- **60% training:** fit preprocessing and model parameters;
- **15% calibration:** fit optional probability calibration;
- **10% validation:** select the probability model and the threshold rule;
- **15% test:** final evaluation after choices are locked.

```{r split-functions}
stratified_four_way_split <- function(y, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)

  parts <- list(
    train = integer(),
    calibration = integer(),
    validation = integer(),
    test = integer()
  )

  for (cls in sort(unique(y))) {
    ids <- sample(which(y == cls))
    n <- length(ids)

    n_train <- floor(0.60 * n)
    n_cal <- floor(0.15 * n)
    n_val <- floor(0.10 * n)

    parts$train <- c(parts$train, ids[seq_len(n_train)])
    parts$calibration <- c(
      parts$calibration,
      ids[(n_train + 1):(n_train + n_cal)]
    )
    parts$validation <- c(
      parts$validation,
      ids[(n_train + n_cal + 1):(n_train + n_cal + n_val)]
    )
    parts$test <- c(
      parts$test,
      ids[(n_train + n_cal + n_val + 1):n]
    )
  }

  lapply(parts, sort)
}

ids <- stratified_four_way_split(y, params$seed)

split_table <- data.frame(
  Subset = names(ids),
  Loans = vapply(ids, length, integer(1)),
  DefaultRate = vapply(ids, function(i) mean(y[i]), numeric(1))
)

split_table$DefaultRate <- sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * split_table$DefaultRate)

paper_kable(
  split_table,
  caption = "Development partitions."
)
```

This design assumes each row is an independent loan. If repeated borrower IDs or origination dates become available, a borrower-grouped or out-of-time design would be preferable.

## Leakage-Safe Preprocessing

Preprocessing is learned **only on the training subset**.

```{r preprocessing}
fit_recipe <- function(training_x) {
  recipes::recipe(~ ., data = training_x) |>
    recipes::step_impute_median(recipes::all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    recipes::step_unknown(recipes::all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    recipes::step_novel(recipes::all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    recipes::step_dummy(recipes::all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    recipes::step_zv(recipes::all_predictors()) |>
    recipes::step_normalize(recipes::all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    recipes::prep(training = training_x, retain = FALSE)
}

rec <- fit_recipe(X_raw[ids$train, , drop = FALSE])

bake_x <- function(i) {
  as.data.frame(
    recipes::bake(
      rec,
      new_data = X_raw[i, , drop = FALSE]
    )
  )
}

X_train <- bake_x(ids$train)
X_cal <- bake_x(ids$calibration)
X_val <- bake_x(ids$validation)
X_test <- bake_x(ids$test)

y_train <- y[ids$train]
y_cal <- y[ids$calibration]
y_val <- y[ids$validation]
y_test <- y[ids$test]
```

Standardization is useful for regularized optimization because predictors on very different numerical scales can create poor conditioning and unstable numerical behavior.

## Candidate Models

The candidate set contains models with different levels of flexibility.

| Model | Statistical role |
|:--|:--|
| Logistic regression | Interpretable linear log-odds baseline |
| Ridge logistic regression | Logistic model with coefficient shrinkage |
| Random forest | Nonlinear tree ensemble |
| Gradient boosting | Sequential nonlinear ensemble |
| Neural network (optional) | Flexible nonlinear composition |

The purpose of including more complex models is not to assume they are superior. Flexible models are retained only when they demonstrate stronger held-out predictive performance, because additional flexibility can also increase overfitting risk.

### Probability-Loss Criterion

For a binary outcome, the validation log loss is

\[
-\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
y_i \log(\widehat p_i)
+
(1-y_i)\log(1-\widehat p_i)
\right].
\]

This is the negative average Bernoulli log-likelihood. Because this project is intended to estimate probabilities, log loss is the **primary model-selection criterion**.

Brier score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC are used as supporting diagnostics.

```{r metric-functions}
clip_p <- function(p) {
  pmax(1e-6, pmin(1 - 1e-6, as.numeric(p)))
}

logloss <- function(y, p) {
  p <- clip_p(p)
  -mean(y * log(p) + (1-y) * log1p(-p))
}

brier <- function(y, p) {
  mean((clip_p(p) - y)^2)
}

probability_metrics <- function(y, p) {
  p <- clip_p(p)

  truth <- factor(
    ifelse(y == 1, "default", "non_default"),
    levels = c("default","non_default")
  )

  data.frame(
    LogLoss = logloss(y, p),
    Brier = brier(y, p),
    ROC_AUC = yardstick::roc_auc_vec(
      truth = truth,
      estimate = p,
      event_level = "first"
    ),
    PR_AUC = yardstick::pr_auc_vec(
      truth = truth,
      estimate = p,
      event_level = "first"
    )
  )
}

fit_platt <- function(p, y) {
  z <- qlogis(clip_p(p))

  fit <- glm(
    y ~ z,
    family = binomial(),
    data = data.frame(y = y, z = z)
  )

  fit
}

apply_platt <- function(fit, p) {
  clip_p(
    predict(
      fit,
      newdata = data.frame(z = qlogis(clip_p(p))),
      type = "response"
    )
  )
}
```

## Model Fitting and Optimization

Statistical estimation can be expressed as an optimization problem. Logistic regression optimizes Bernoulli likelihood; ridge regression adds a penalty; boosting and neural networks optimize loss numerically.


```{r fit-models, results='hide'}
model_cache <- file.path(
  params$output_dir,
  "stat8670_models_and_predictions.rds"
)

need_fit <- isTRUE(params$force_retrain) || !file.exists(model_cache)

if (need_fit) {

  train_glm <- data.frame(Default = y_train, X_train)
  logistic_fit <- glm(
    Default ~ .,
    data = train_glm,
    family = binomial()
  )

  pred_logistic <- function(newx) {
    clip_p(
      predict(
        logistic_fit,
        newdata = newx,
        type = "response"
      )
    )
  }

  set.seed(params$seed)
  ridge_cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(
    x = as.matrix(X_train),
    y = y_train,
    family = "binomial",
    alpha = 0,
    nfolds = 5,
    standardize = FALSE,
    type.measure = "deviance"
  )

  pred_ridge <- function(newx) {
    clip_p(
      as.numeric(
        predict(
          ridge_cv,
          newx = as.matrix(newx),
          s = "lambda.min",
          type = "response"
        )
      )
    )
  }

  train_rf <- data.frame(
    Default = factor(
      ifelse(y_train == 1, "default", "non_default"),
      levels = c("non_default","default")
    ),
    X_train
  )

  rf_grid <- data.frame(
    mtry = unique(pmax(
      1L,
      c(
        floor(sqrt(ncol(X_train))),
        floor(ncol(X_train)/3),
        floor(ncol(X_train)/2)
      )
    )),
    min.node.size = c(50L,100L,200L)[seq_along(
      unique(pmax(
        1L,
        c(
          floor(sqrt(ncol(X_train))),
          floor(ncol(X_train)/3),
          floor(ncol(X_train)/2)
        )
      ))
    )]
  )

  rf_fits <- vector("list", nrow(rf_grid))

  for (j in seq_len(nrow(rf_grid))) {
    rf_fits[[j]] <- ranger::ranger(
      Default ~ .,
      data = train_rf,
      probability = TRUE,
      num.trees = 350,
      mtry = rf_grid$mtry[j],
      min.node.size = rf_grid$min.node.size[j],
      seed = params$seed + j,
      num.threads = 2,
      importance = "none",
      verbose = FALSE
    )
  }

  rf_val_loss <- vapply(
    rf_fits,
    function(m) {
      p <- predict(m, data = X_val)$predictions[, "default"]
      logloss(y_val, p)
    },
    numeric(1)
  )

  rf_fit <- rf_fits[[which.min(rf_val_loss)]]

  pred_rf <- function(newx) {
    clip_p(
      predict(
        rf_fit,
        data = newx,
        num.threads = 1
      )$predictions[, "default"]
    )
  }

  train_gbm <- data.frame(Default = y_train, X_train)

  gbm_grid <- expand.grid(
    depth = c(1,2,3),
    shrinkage = c(0.03,0.06),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  gbm_fits <- vector("list", nrow(gbm_grid))
  gbm_val_loss <- numeric(nrow(gbm_grid))

  for (j in seq_len(nrow(gbm_grid))) {
    set.seed(params$seed + 100 + j)

    gbm_fits[[j]] <- gbm::gbm(
      Default ~ .,
      distribution = "bernoulli",
      data = train_gbm,
      n.trees = 600,
      interaction.depth = gbm_grid$depth[j],
      shrinkage = gbm_grid$shrinkage[j],
      n.minobsinnode = 50,
      bag.fraction = 0.7,
      train.fraction = 1,
      verbose = FALSE
    )

    p <- predict(
      gbm_fits[[j]],
      newdata = X_val,
      n.trees = 600,
      type = "response"
    )

    gbm_val_loss[j] <- logloss(y_val, p)
  }

  gbm_fit <- gbm_fits[[which.min(gbm_val_loss)]]

  pred_gbm <- function(newx) {
    clip_p(
      predict(
        gbm_fit,
        newdata = newx,
        n.trees = 600,
        type = "response"
      )
    )
  }

  models <- list(
    logistic = list(
      fit = logistic_fit,
      predict_fun = pred_logistic,
      complexity = 1
    ),
    ridge = list(
      fit = ridge_cv,
      predict_fun = pred_ridge,
      complexity = 2
    ),
    random_forest = list(
      fit = rf_fit,
      predict_fun = pred_rf,
      complexity = 3
    ),
    boosting = list(
      fit = gbm_fit,
      predict_fun = pred_gbm,
      complexity = 3
    )
  )

  if (isTRUE(params$include_neural)) {

    if (!requireNamespace("keras3", quietly = TRUE)) {
      stop(
        "include_neural=TRUE requires keras3. ",
        "Install and configure keras3 before knitting."
      )
    }

    set.seed(params$seed)

    nn <- keras3::keras_model_sequential() |>
      keras3::layer_dense(
        units = 32,
        activation = "relu",
        input_shape = ncol(X_train)
      ) |>
      keras3::layer_dropout(rate = 0.15) |>
      keras3::layer_dense(
        units = 16,
        activation = "relu"
      ) |>
      keras3::layer_dense(
        units = 1,
        activation = "sigmoid"
      )

    nn |>
      keras3::compile(
        optimizer = keras3::optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.001),
        loss = "binary_crossentropy"
      )

    nn |>
      keras3::fit(
        x = as.matrix(X_train),
        y = y_train,
        validation_data = list(
          as.matrix(X_val),
          y_val
        ),
        epochs = 40,
        batch_size = 512,
        callbacks = list(
          keras3::callback_early_stopping(
            monitor = "val_loss",
            patience = 4,
            restore_best_weights = TRUE
          )
        ),
        verbose = 0
      )

    pred_nn <- function(newx) {
      clip_p(
        as.numeric(
          predict(
            nn,
            as.matrix(newx),
            verbose = 0
          )
        )
      )
    }

    models$neural_network <- list(
      fit = nn,
      predict_fun = pred_nn,
      complexity = 4
    )
  }

  model_eval <- list()
  calibrators <- list()
  prediction_store <- list()

  for (nm in names(models)) {

    p_cal_raw <- models[[nm]]$predict_fun(X_cal)
    platt <- fit_platt(p_cal_raw, y_cal)

    p_val_raw <- models[[nm]]$predict_fun(X_val)
    p_val_platt <- apply_platt(platt, p_val_raw)

    raw_metrics <- probability_metrics(y_val, p_val_raw)
    cal_metrics <- probability_metrics(y_val, p_val_platt)

    model_eval[[paste0(nm, "__raw")]] <- cbind(
      Model = nm,
      Calibration = "raw",
      raw_metrics
    )

    model_eval[[paste0(nm, "__platt")]] <- cbind(
      Model = nm,
      Calibration = "platt",
      cal_metrics
    )

    calibrators[[nm]] <- platt

    prediction_store[[nm]] <- list(
      validation_raw = p_val_raw,
      validation_platt = p_val_platt,
      test_raw = models[[nm]]$predict_fun(X_test)
    )
  }

  comparison <- do.call(rbind, model_eval)
  rownames(comparison) <- NULL
  comparison <- comparison[order(
    comparison$LogLoss,
    comparison$Brier
  ), ]

  min_loss <- min(comparison$LogLoss)
  near_best <- comparison[
    comparison$LogLoss <= min_loss + 0.001,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  complexity_lookup <- vapply(
    models,
    function(z) z$complexity,
    numeric(1)
  )

  near_best$ComplexityRank <- complexity_lookup[near_best$Model]

  selected_row <- near_best[
    order(
      near_best$ComplexityRank,
      near_best$LogLoss,
      near_best$Brier
    ),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ][1, ]

  selected_name <- selected_row$Model
  selected_calibration <- selected_row$Calibration

  selected_model <- models[[selected_name]]

  selected_platt <- if (selected_calibration == "platt") {
    calibrators[[selected_name]]
  } else {
    NULL
  }

  selected_probability <- function(newx) {
    p <- selected_model$predict_fun(newx)

    if (!is.null(selected_platt)) {
      p <- apply_platt(selected_platt, p)
    }

    clip_p(p)
  }

  p_val <- selected_probability(X_val)
  p_test <- selected_probability(X_test)

  saveRDS(
    list(
      models = models,
      calibrators = calibrators,
      comparison = comparison,
      selected_name = selected_name,
      selected_calibration = selected_calibration,
      p_val = p_val,
      p_test = p_test,
      rec = rec,
      ids = ids
    ),
    model_cache
  )

} else {

  cached <- readRDS(model_cache)

  models <- cached$models
  calibrators <- cached$calibrators
  comparison <- cached$comparison
  selected_name <- cached$selected_name
  selected_calibration <- cached$selected_calibration
  p_val <- cached$p_val
  p_test <- cached$p_test
  rec <- cached$rec
  ids <- cached$ids

  # Rebuild baked partitions consistently.
  X_train <- as.data.frame(
    recipes::bake(rec, new_data = X_raw[ids$train, , drop = FALSE])
  )
  X_cal <- as.data.frame(
    recipes::bake(rec, new_data = X_raw[ids$calibration, , drop = FALSE])
  )
  X_val <- as.data.frame(
    recipes::bake(rec, new_data = X_raw[ids$validation, , drop = FALSE])
  )
  X_test <- as.data.frame(
    recipes::bake(rec, new_data = X_raw[ids$test, , drop = FALSE])
  )

  y_train <- y[ids$train]
  y_cal <- y[ids$calibration]
  y_val <- y[ids$validation]
  y_test <- y[ids$test]
}
```


```{r candidate-prediction-helper, include=FALSE}
predict_candidate_raw <- function(model_name, newx) {
  m <- models[[model_name]]$fit

  if (model_name == "logistic") {
    return(clip_p(predict(m, newdata = newx, type = "response")))
  }

  if (model_name == "ridge") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        as.numeric(
          predict(
            m,
            newx = as.matrix(newx),
            s = "lambda.min",
            type = "response"
          )
        )
      )
    )
  }

  if (model_name == "random_forest") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        predict(
          m,
          data = newx,
          num.threads = 1
        )$predictions[, "default"]
      )
    )
  }

  if (model_name == "boosting") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        predict(
          m,
          newdata = newx,
          n.trees = 600,
          type = "response"
        )
      )
    )
  }

  if (model_name == "neural_network") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        as.numeric(
          predict(
            m,
            as.matrix(newx),
            verbose = 0
          )
        )
      )
    )
  }

  stop("Unknown model candidate: ", model_name)
}

candidate_probability <- function(model_name, calibration, newx) {
  p <- predict_candidate_raw(model_name, newx)

  if (calibration == "platt") {
    p <- apply_platt(calibrators[[model_name]], p)
  }

  clip_p(p)
}
```


## Deployment-Stability Simulation Design

The empirical analysis provides an internally validated reference model but cannot identify how model behavior changes under a genuinely different deployment population. A controlled Monte Carlo design is therefore used to study distribution shift while keeping the relevant data-generating mechanisms known.

### Baseline data-generating mechanism

Three independent standardized predictors are generated as

\[
X_1,X_2,X_3\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1),
\]

with binary outcome

\[
Y_i\mid X_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i),
\]

and baseline logistic mechanism

\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_i)
=
\beta_0+0.8X_{i1}-0.6X_{i2}+0.4X_{i3}.
\]

The intercept is selected so that baseline event prevalence is approximately 12%, close to the empirical default rate. The slopes \(0.8\), \(-0.6\), and \(0.4\) are simulation design parameters chosen to create moderate effects of different magnitudes and directions; they are not estimates from the empirical loan data.

Each condition uses \(R=500\) Monte Carlo replications with simulation seed 1998. Unless otherwise stated, training, validation/adaptation, and test samples contain 5,000 observations. Fresh samples are generated within each replication. The fitted model is ordinary logistic regression.

Before introducing shift, a coefficient-recovery experiment verifies the implementation under correct specification. Across 500 replications, the mean estimates were \(-2.3903\), \(0.8030\), \(-0.6028\), and \(0.3991\) for true values \(-2.387\), \(0.8\), \(-0.6\), and \(0.4\), respectively.

### Probability, discrimination, and calibration measures

Because the true data-generating probabilities are known in simulation, the fitted model can be compared with an oracle using the true deployment probabilities. Probability accuracy is summarized by log loss, Brier score, and

\[
\operatorname{PMSE}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(\widehat p_i-p_i^{\mathrm{true}})^2.
\]

Excess log loss and excess Brier score are calculated relative to the oracle so that changes in population composition or intrinsic prediction difficulty are not confused with model error.

Discrimination is measured by ROC-AUC. Calibration is summarized by the logistic calibration model

\[
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y=1)\}
=
a+b\,\operatorname{logit}(\widehat p),
\]

where ideal calibration corresponds to intercept \(a=0\) and slope \(b=1\).

### Covariate shift and misspecification

The first experiment changes the deployment distribution of \(X_1\):

\[
X_1^{\mathrm{deploy}}\sim N(\delta,1),
\qquad
\delta\in\{0,0.5,1,1.5,2\},
\]

while \(X_2\) and \(X_3\) remain standard normal. The conditional outcome mechanism is held fixed, so this is pure covariate shift.

To examine the interaction between shift and model misspecification, the true mechanism is extended to

\[
\operatorname{logit}(p)
=
\beta_0+0.8X_1-0.6X_2+0.4X_3+\beta_4X_1^2,
\]

with

\[
\beta_4\in\{0,0.25,0.50\}.
\]

For each value of \(\beta_4\), the intercept is recalibrated so that baseline prevalence at \(\delta=0\) remains approximately 12%. The fitted logistic model deliberately omits \(X_1^2\). Thus \(\beta_4=0\) is the correctly specified control condition, while \(0.25\) and \(0.50\) represent moderate and stronger misspecification.

### Decision-threshold stability

For each misspecification condition and replication, the fitted model is trained on the baseline population. An independent baseline validation sample at \(\delta=0\) selects the threshold maximizing balanced accuracy over the prespecified grid \(0.01,0.015,\ldots,0.50\). For each deployment value of \(\delta\), a separate shifted adaptation sample estimates the deployment-optimal threshold, and an independent shifted test sample evaluates both the frozen baseline threshold and the adapted threshold.

This design separates threshold selection from threshold evaluation. The main quantities are threshold movement and the balanced-accuracy gain from adaptation.

### Intercept outcome shift

The second outcome-mechanism experiment leaves the predictor distribution and slopes unchanged but adds a deployment intercept shift,

\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_{\mathrm{deploy}})
=
\beta_0+\gamma+0.8X_1-0.6X_2+0.4X_3,
\]

where

\[
\gamma\in\{0,0.25,0.50,0.75,1\}.
\]

The original fitted model is not updated. Because

\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_{\mathrm{deploy}})
=
\gamma+\operatorname{logit}(p_{\mathrm{baseline}}),
\]

the population calibration relationship is expected to have intercept \(a=\gamma\) and slope \(b=1\).

### Slope outcome shift

The final experiment changes the true deployment effect of \(X_1\):

\[
\beta_{1,\mathrm{deploy}}=0.8-\kappa,
\]

with

\[
\kappa\in\{0,0.4,0.8,1.2,1.6\}.
\]

The deployment coefficient therefore moves from \(0.8\) to \(0.4\), \(0\), \(-0.4\), and \(-0.8\). For each condition, the deployment intercept is recalibrated to keep event prevalence near 12%. This isolates deterioration caused by a changing predictor--outcome relationship rather than by a large prevalence change.

### Monte Carlo uncertainty

For a simulation summary \(\bar\theta\), Monte Carlo standard error is

\[
\operatorname{MCSE}(\bar\theta)
=
\frac{s_\theta}{\sqrt{R}},
\]

where \(s_\theta\) is the empirical standard deviation across the \(R=500\) replications. MCSE quantifies numerical uncertainty from the finite number of simulation runs; it is not an uncertainty interval for real-world deployment performance.

\clearpage

# Results

## Validation-Based Model Selection

```{r validation-model-comparison}
comparison_display <- comparison |>
  arrange(LogLoss, Brier) |>
  mutate(
    Model = recode(
      Model,
      logistic = "Logistic regression",
      ridge = "Ridge logistic",
      random_forest = "Random forest",
      boosting = "Gradient boosting"
    ),
    Calibration = recode(Calibration, raw = "Raw", platt = "Platt"),
    across(
      c(LogLoss,Brier,ROC_AUC,PR_AUC),
      ~ round(.x, 4)
    )
  )

paper_kable(
  comparison_display,
  caption = "Validation probability performance. Lower LogLoss and Brier are better; higher ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are better."
)
```

```{r validation-model-plot}
plot_comp <- comparison |>
  mutate(
    Candidate = paste(Model, Calibration, sep = " + ")
  ) |>
  arrange(LogLoss)

ggplot(
  plot_comp,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Candidate, LogLoss),
    y = LogLoss
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Validation Log Loss by Candidate",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Validation log loss"
  )
```

The lowest validation log loss was obtained by **`r selected_name`** with **`r selected_calibration`** probabilities.

Selection is based primarily on validation log loss because the target of interest is a probability. A prespecified parsimony rule is used when candidates are practically tied within 0.001 log-loss units: the simpler candidate is preferred when additional complexity does not produce a meaningful validation improvement.


### Bootstrap Stability of the Validation Ranking

A single validation table reports one realized comparison. To assess whether the ranking is fragile to the particular validation observations, the fitted candidate models are held fixed and the validation set is bootstrap-resampled. This is a **conditional stability analysis of the validation ranking**; it is not a substitute for a completely new external sample or repeated refitting on new development splits.

```{r validation-ranking-stability}
candidate_labels <- paste(
  comparison$Model,
  comparison$Calibration,
  sep = " + "
)

candidate_predictions <- lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(comparison)),
  function(i) {
    candidate_probability(
      comparison$Model[i],
      comparison$Calibration[i],
      X_val
    )
  }
)

names(candidate_predictions) <- candidate_labels

B_rank <- max(100L, as.integer(params$bootstrap_reps))
set.seed(params$seed + 801L)

rank_boot <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = B_rank,
  ncol = length(candidate_predictions),
  dimnames = list(NULL, names(candidate_predictions))
)

for (b in seq_len(B_rank)) {
  ix <- sample.int(length(y_val), replace = TRUE)

  rank_boot[b, ] <- vapply(
    candidate_predictions,
    function(p) logloss(y_val[ix], p[ix]),
    numeric(1)
  )
}

winner <- apply(
  rank_boot,
  1,
  function(z) names(z)[which.min(z)]
)

selection_stability <- data.frame(
  Candidate = names(candidate_predictions),
  BootstrapSelectionRate = vapply(
    names(candidate_predictions),
    function(nm) mean(winner == nm),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  MeanBootstrapLogLoss = colMeans(rank_boot),
  SDLogLoss = apply(rank_boot, 2, sd)
) |>
  arrange(desc(BootstrapSelectionRate), MeanBootstrapLogLoss)

bootstrap_stability_display <- selection_stability |>
  transmute(
    Candidate,
    `Selection rate` = scales::percent(BootstrapSelectionRate, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Mean log loss` = round(MeanBootstrapLogLoss, 5),
    `SD` = round(SDLogLoss, 5)
  )

paper_kable(
  bootstrap_stability_display,
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l","r","r","r"),
  caption = "Bootstrap stability of the validation model ranking, conditional on the fitted candidate models."
)
```

```{r validation-ranking-stability-plot, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=3.6, out.width='78%'}
ggplot(
  selection_stability,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Candidate, BootstrapSelectionRate),
    y = BootstrapSelectionRate
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Stability of Validation Model Selection",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of bootstrap validation samples selected"
  )
```

A high bootstrap selection rate for the retained candidate indicates that its validation advantage is not driven only by a small number of observations. A diffuse distribution of selection rates would instead indicate that the candidate models are practically difficult to distinguish with the available validation evidence.


## Decision-Threshold Optimization

Probability estimation and classification are treated as different steps. A different threshold can be appropriate when the consequences of false positives and false negatives differ.

For comparison, an F2-based objective is also evaluated. Because F2 weights recall more strongly than precision, it generally favors a lower cutoff and a larger review set.

The primary threshold objective is **balanced accuracy** because verified economic costs are unavailable:

\[
\text{Balanced Accuracy}
=
\frac{\text{Recall}+\text{Specificity}}{2},
\]

which treats sensitivity and specificity symmetrically.

This should not be interpreted as a universal lending-policy optimum. If real false-negative and false-positive costs become available, expected cost should replace a generic statistical objective.

```{r threshold-analysis}
threshold_metrics <- function(y, p, thresholds = seq(0.01, 0.40, by = 0.0025)) {

  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(thresholds, function(t) {

      flag <- p >= t

      TP <- sum(flag & y == 1)
      FP <- sum(flag & y == 0)
      TN <- sum(!flag & y == 0)
      FN <- sum(!flag & y == 1)

      recall <- if ((TP + FN) > 0) TP / (TP + FN) else NA_real_
      precision <- if ((TP + FP) > 0) TP / (TP + FP) else NA_real_
      specificity <- if ((TN + FP) > 0) TN / (TN + FP) else NA_real_

      f1 <- if ((2*TP + FP + FN) > 0) {
        2*TP / (2*TP + FP + FN)
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }

      f2 <- if ((5*TP + 4*FN + FP) > 0) {
        5*TP / (5*TP + 4*FN + FP)
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }

      data.frame(
        Threshold = t,
        Recall = recall,
        Precision = precision,
        Specificity = specificity,
        FalsePositiveRate = 1 - specificity,
        FlaggedRate = mean(flag),
        F1 = f1,
        F2 = f2,
        BalancedAccuracy = mean(c(recall, specificity), na.rm = TRUE),
        YoudenJ = recall + specificity - 1,
        TP = TP,
        FP = FP,
        TN = TN,
        FN = FN
      )
    })
  )
}

val_thresholds <- threshold_metrics(y_val, p_val)

objective <- tolower(params$threshold_objective)

if (objective == "balanced_accuracy") {
  best_i <- which.max(val_thresholds$BalancedAccuracy)
} else if (objective == "f1") {
  best_i <- which.max(val_thresholds$F1)
} else if (objective == "f2") {
  best_i <- which.max(val_thresholds$F2)
} else if (objective == "youden") {
  best_i <- which.max(val_thresholds$YoudenJ)
} else {
  stop(
    "threshold_objective must be one of: ",
    "balanced_accuracy, f1, f2, youden"
  )
}

selected_threshold <- val_thresholds$Threshold[best_i]

threshold_objective_summary <- data.frame(
  Objective = c(
    "F2",
    "F1",
    "Balanced accuracy",
    "Youden J"
  ),
  Threshold = c(
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$F2)],
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$F1)],
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$BalancedAccuracy)],
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$YoudenJ)]
  )
)

threshold_objective_summary$Threshold <- sprintf(
  "%.1f%%",
  100 * threshold_objective_summary$Threshold
)

paper_kable(
  threshold_objective_summary,
  caption = "Validation-selected thresholds under different statistical objectives."
)
```

```{r threshold-curves}
threshold_long <- val_thresholds |>
  select(
    Threshold,
    Recall,
    Precision,
    Specificity,
    FalsePositiveRate,
    FlaggedRate
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -Threshold,
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Rate"
  )

ggplot(
  threshold_long,
  aes(
    x = Threshold,
    y = Rate,
    linetype = Metric
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = selected_threshold,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Validation Threshold Trade-off",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Dashed line = ",
      params$threshold_objective,
      " selected cutoff"
    ),
    x = "Review threshold",
    y = "Rate",
    linetype = NULL
  )
```

The chosen threshold is **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*selected_threshold)`** under the declared **`r params$threshold_objective`** objective.

The threshold was selected **only on validation data**. The test set was not used to tune it.


### Sensitivity to the Threshold Objective

Balanced accuracy is the primary threshold objective because verified monetary error costs are unavailable. To show that the operating rule depends on the objective rather than on the probability model, four thresholds are selected independently on validation data and then evaluated on the locked test set.

```{r threshold-objective-sensitivity}
threshold_choice <- data.frame(
  Objective = c("F2","F1","Balanced accuracy","Youden J"),
  Threshold = c(
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$F2)],
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$F1)],
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$BalancedAccuracy)],
    val_thresholds$Threshold[which.max(val_thresholds$YoudenJ)]
  )
)

threshold_class_metrics <- function(y, p, threshold) {
  flag <- p >= threshold
  TP <- sum(flag & y == 1)
  FP <- sum(flag & y == 0)
  TN <- sum(!flag & y == 0)
  FN <- sum(!flag & y == 1)

  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold,
    Recall = if ((TP + FN) > 0) TP/(TP + FN) else NA_real_,
    Precision = if ((TP + FP) > 0) TP/(TP + FP) else NA_real_,
    Specificity = if ((TN + FP) > 0) TN/(TN + FP) else NA_real_,
    FalsePositiveRate = if ((FP + TN) > 0) FP/(FP + TN) else NA_real_,
    FlaggedRate = mean(flag),
    Accuracy = (TP + TN)/length(y),
    TP = TP, FP = FP, TN = TN, FN = FN
  )
}

threshold_test_rows <- lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(threshold_choice)),
  function(i) {
    z <- threshold_class_metrics(
      y_test,
      p_test,
      threshold_choice$Threshold[i]
    )

    cbind(
      Objective = threshold_choice$Objective[i],
      z
    )
  }
)

threshold_test_comparison <- do.call(
  rbind,
  threshold_test_rows
)

threshold_test_display <- threshold_test_comparison |>
  select(
    Objective, Threshold, Recall, Precision,
    Specificity, FalsePositiveRate, FlaggedRate, Accuracy
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        Threshold, Recall, Precision, Specificity,
        FalsePositiveRate, FlaggedRate, Accuracy
      ),
      ~ round(.x, 4)
    )
  )

paper_kable(
  threshold_test_display |>
    select(
      Objective, Threshold, Recall,
      Precision, Specificity
    ),
  caption = "Test sensitivity, precision, and specificity under validation-selected threshold objectives."
)

paper_kable(
  threshold_test_display |>
    select(
      Objective, FalsePositiveRate,
      FlaggedRate, Accuracy
    ),
  caption = "Test review burden and overall accuracy under validation-selected threshold objectives."
)
```

This comparison is not intended to identify a universally optimal cutoff. It demonstrates that the operating point depends on the chosen loss or utility criterion. In a production setting, verified economic costs or review-capacity constraints should replace a generic statistical threshold objective.


## Held-Out Test Performance

```{r test-metrics}
class_metrics <- function(y, p, threshold) {

  flag <- p >= threshold

  TP <- sum(flag & y == 1)
  FP <- sum(flag & y == 0)
  TN <- sum(!flag & y == 0)
  FN <- sum(!flag & y == 1)

  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold,
    Recall = TP / (TP + FN),
    Precision = if ((TP + FP) > 0) TP/(TP+FP) else NA_real_,
    Specificity = TN/(TN+FP),
    FalsePositiveRate = FP/(FP+TN),
    FlaggedRate = mean(flag),
    Accuracy = (TP+TN)/length(y),
    TP = TP,
    FP = FP,
    TN = TN,
    FN = FN
  )
}

test_prob <- probability_metrics(y_test, p_test)
test_class <- class_metrics(y_test, p_test, selected_threshold)

test_summary <- cbind(
  Model = paste(selected_name, selected_calibration, sep = " + "),
  test_prob,
  test_class
)

test_probability_display <- test_summary |>
  select(Model, LogLoss, Brier, ROC_AUC, PR_AUC) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(LogLoss, Brier, ROC_AUC, PR_AUC),
      ~ round(as.numeric(.x), 4)
    )
  )

test_operating_display <- test_summary |>
  select(
    Threshold, Recall, Precision, Specificity,
    FalsePositiveRate, FlaggedRate, Accuracy,
    TP, FP, TN, FN
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        Threshold, Recall, Precision, Specificity,
        FalsePositiveRate, FlaggedRate, Accuracy
      ),
      ~ round(as.numeric(.x), 4)
    )
  )

paper_kable(
  test_probability_display,
  caption = "Held-out test probability performance."
)

paper_kable(
  test_operating_display[, c(
    "Threshold","Recall","Precision","Specificity",
    "FalsePositiveRate","FlaggedRate","Accuracy"
  )],
  caption = "Held-out test operating characteristics at the validation-selected threshold."
)

paper_kable(
  test_operating_display[, c("TP","FP","TN","FN")],
  caption = "Held-out test confusion-matrix counts."
)
```

This table is the final generalization assessment for the selected probability model and validation-selected threshold.


### Bootstrap Uncertainty for Final Test Metrics

Point estimates can conceal sampling uncertainty. The following intervals bootstrap the **locked test observations** while holding the fitted model and threshold fixed. They quantify uncertainty in the reported test metrics; they do not account for uncertainty arising from an entirely new model-development sample.

```{r test-bootstrap-ci, results='asis'}
test_metric_vector <- function(y, p, threshold) {
  prob <- probability_metrics(y, p)
  cls <- class_metrics(y, p, threshold)

  c(
    ROC_AUC = prob$ROC_AUC,
    PR_AUC = prob$PR_AUC,
    Brier = prob$Brier,
    LogLoss = prob$LogLoss,
    Recall = cls$Recall,
    Precision = cls$Precision,
    Specificity = cls$Specificity,
    FalsePositiveRate = cls$FalsePositiveRate,
    FlaggedRate = cls$FlaggedRate,
    Accuracy = cls$Accuracy
  )
}

B_test <- max(100L, as.integer(params$bootstrap_reps))
set.seed(params$seed + 901L)

boot_test <- replicate(
  B_test,
  {
    ix <- sample.int(length(y_test), replace = TRUE)
    test_metric_vector(
      y_test[ix],
      p_test[ix],
      selected_threshold
    )
  }
)

boot_test <- t(boot_test)

point <- test_metric_vector(
  y_test,
  p_test,
  selected_threshold
)

ci_table <- data.frame(
  Metric = names(point),
  Estimate = as.numeric(point),
  Lower95 = apply(
    boot_test,
    2,
    quantile,
    probs = 0.025,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ),
  Upper95 = apply(
    boot_test,
    2,
    quantile,
    probs = 0.975,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
)

ci_display <- ci_table |>
  transmute(
    Metric,
    Estimate = round(Estimate, 4),
    `Lower 95%` = round(Lower95, 4),
    `Upper 95%` = round(Upper95, 4)
  )

knitr::kable(
  ci_display,
  format = "pipe",
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Bootstrap 95% intervals for locked test performance."
)
```

## Calibration

A useful risk model should not only rank loans correctly; its probabilities should also correspond reasonably to observed frequencies.

```{r calibration}
calibration_table <- function(y, p, groups = 10) {

  qs <- unique(
    quantile(
      p,
      probs = seq(0,1,length.out = groups+1),
      type = 8
    )
  )

  if (length(qs) < 3) {
    return(
      data.frame(
        Group = "All",
        N = length(y),
        MeanPredicted = mean(p),
        ObservedDefaultRate = mean(y)
      )
    )
  }

  qs[1] <- -Inf
  qs[length(qs)] <- Inf

  g <- cut(
    p,
    breaks = qs,
    include.lowest = TRUE
  )

  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(
      split(seq_along(y), g),
      function(i) {
        data.frame(
          Group = as.character(g[i[1]]),
          N = length(i),
          MeanPredicted = mean(p[i]),
          ObservedDefaultRate = mean(y[i])
        )
      }
    )
  )
}

cal_test <- calibration_table(y_test, p_test)

calibration_display <- cal_test |>
  transmute(
    `Risk group` = Group,
    N,
    `Mean predicted` = round(MeanPredicted, 4),
    `Observed default rate` = round(ObservedDefaultRate, 4)
  )

paper_kable(
  calibration_display,
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l","r","r","r"),
  caption = "Held-out calibration by risk group."
)
```

```{r calibration-plot, fig.width=5.4, fig.height=3.3, out.width='72%'}
ggplot(
  cal_test,
  aes(
    x = MeanPredicted,
    y = ObservedDefaultRate,
    size = N
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Held-out Calibration",
    x = "Mean predicted probability",
    y = "Observed default rate",
    size = "Loans"
  )
```


### Calibration Intercept and Slope

The grouped calibration plot provides a visual diagnostic. Two additional summaries are estimated on the locked test set. A calibration intercept near 0 indicates correct average risk, while a calibration slope near 1 indicates that the spread of predicted risks is appropriate.

```{r calibration-intercept-slope}
lp_test <- qlogis(clip_p(p_test))

cal_intercept_fit <- glm(
  y_test ~ 1,
  offset = lp_test,
  family = binomial()
)

cal_slope_fit <- glm(
  y_test ~ lp_test,
  family = binomial()
)

calibration_summary <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Calibration-in-the-large intercept",
    "Calibration model intercept",
    "Calibration slope"
  ),
  Estimate = c(
    unname(coef(cal_intercept_fit)[1]),
    unname(coef(cal_slope_fit)[1]),
    unname(coef(cal_slope_fit)["lp_test"])
  ),
  Reference = c(0,0,1)
)

paper_kable(
  calibration_summary |>
    mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 4)),
  caption = "Calibration intercept and slope on the locked test set."
)
```

These quantities should be interpreted together with the calibration curve and Brier/log-loss results rather than as stand-alone pass/fail tests.

## Predictor Reliance

Permutation importance evaluates how much validation log loss increases when one predictor is randomly disrupted.

This measures **predictive reliance**, not causal effect.

```{r permutation-importance}
selected_model_cached <- models[[selected_name]]

# Rebuild selected prediction rule from cached model objects.
predict_selected_raw <- function(newx) {

  if (selected_name == "logistic") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        predict(
          selected_model_cached$fit,
          newdata = newx,
          type = "response"
        )
      )
    )
  }

  if (selected_name == "ridge") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        as.numeric(
          predict(
            selected_model_cached$fit,
            newx = as.matrix(newx),
            s = "lambda.min",
            type = "response"
          )
        )
      )
    )
  }

  if (selected_name == "random_forest") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        predict(
          selected_model_cached$fit,
          data = newx,
          num.threads = 1
        )$predictions[, "default"]
      )
    )
  }

  if (selected_name == "boosting") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        predict(
          selected_model_cached$fit,
          newdata = newx,
          n.trees = 600,
          type = "response"
        )
      )
    )
  }

  if (selected_name == "neural_network") {
    return(
      clip_p(
        as.numeric(
          predict(
            selected_model_cached$fit,
            as.matrix(newx),
            verbose = 0
          )
        )
      )
    )
  }

  stop("Unknown selected model.")
}

selected_calibrator_fit <- if (
  selected_calibration == "platt"
) {
  calibrators[[selected_name]]
} else {
  NULL
}

predict_selected <- function(newx) {
  p <- predict_selected_raw(newx)

  if (!is.null(selected_calibrator_fit)) {
    p <- apply_platt(selected_calibrator_fit, p)
  }

  clip_p(p)
}

base_loss <- logloss(y_val, predict_selected(X_val))

set.seed(params$seed)

importance_rows <- lapply(
  base_features,
  function(feature) {

    altered_raw <- X_raw[ids$validation, , drop = FALSE]

    altered_raw[[feature]] <- sample(
      altered_raw[[feature]],
      nrow(altered_raw)
    )

    # Recompute ratio when one of its constituents changes.
    if (feature %in% c("Income","LoanAmount")) {
      altered_raw$LoanToAnnualIncome <- ifelse(
        altered_raw$Income > 0,
        altered_raw$LoanAmount / altered_raw$Income,
        NA_real_
      )
    }

    altered_baked <- as.data.frame(
      recipes::bake(
        rec,
        new_data = altered_raw
      )
    )

    loss <- logloss(
      y_val,
      predict_selected(altered_baked)
    )

    data.frame(
      Feature = feature,
      IncreaseInLogLoss = loss - base_loss
    )
  }
)

importance <- do.call(rbind, importance_rows) |>
  arrange(desc(IncreaseInLogLoss))

paper_kable(
  importance |>
    mutate(
      IncreaseInLogLoss = round(IncreaseInLogLoss, 5)
    ),
  caption = "Validation permutation importance."
)
```

```{r importance-plot, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.0, out.width='78%'}
ggplot(
  importance,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Feature, IncreaseInLogLoss),
    y = IncreaseInLogLoss
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Predictive Reliance on Validation Data",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Increase in validation log loss"
  )
```

## Age-Related Subgroup and Sensitivity Diagnostics

Previous analysis found that Age can be highly influential. Therefore, Age is examined separately as a diagnostic rather than interpreted causally.

```{r age-group-diagnostic}
age_test <- data.frame(
  Age = loans$Age[ids$test],
  y = y_test,
  p = p_test
)

age_test$AgeGroup <- cut(
  age_test$Age,
  breaks = c(17,24,29,34,39,44,49,54,59,64,Inf),
  labels = c(
    "18-24","25-29","30-34","35-39","40-44",
    "45-49","50-54","55-59","60-64","65+"
  )
)

age_diag <- age_test |>
  group_by(AgeGroup) |>
  summarise(
    Loans = n(),
    Defaults = sum(y == 1),
    NonDefaults = sum(y == 0),
    ObservedDefaultRate = mean(y),
    MeanPredictedRisk = mean(p),
    FlaggedRate = mean(p >= selected_threshold),
    Recall = {
      TP <- sum(p >= selected_threshold & y == 1)
      FN <- sum(p < selected_threshold & y == 1)
      if ((TP + FN) > 0) TP / (TP + FN) else NA_real_
    },
    Specificity = {
      TN <- sum(p < selected_threshold & y == 0)
      FP <- sum(p >= selected_threshold & y == 0)
      if ((TN + FP) > 0) TN / (TN + FP) else NA_real_
    },
    CalibrationGap = mean(y) - mean(p),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

age_diag_display <- age_diag |>
  mutate(
    ObservedDefaultRate = round(ObservedDefaultRate, 4),
    MeanPredictedRisk = round(MeanPredictedRisk, 4),
    FlaggedRate = round(FlaggedRate, 4),
    Recall = round(Recall, 4),
    Specificity = round(Specificity, 4),
    CalibrationGap = round(CalibrationGap, 4)
  )

paper_kable(
  age_diag_display |>
    select(
      AgeGroup, Loans, Defaults,
      ObservedDefaultRate, MeanPredictedRisk,
      CalibrationGap
    ),
  caption = "Age-group observed risk and calibration diagnostic on the held-out test set."
)

paper_kable(
  age_diag_display |>
    select(
      AgeGroup, FlaggedRate,
      Recall, Specificity
    ),
  caption = "Age-group classification behavior at the selected review threshold."
)
```

```{r age-calibration-plot, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=3.4, out.width='78%'}
age_long <- age_diag |>
  select(
    AgeGroup,
    ObservedDefaultRate,
    MeanPredictedRisk
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -AgeGroup,
    names_to = "Measure",
    values_to = "Rate"
  )

ggplot(
  age_long,
  aes(
    x = AgeGroup,
    y = Rate,
    group = Measure,
    linetype = Measure
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Observed and Predicted Risk by Age Group",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Rate",
    linetype = NULL
  )
```

Large differences across age groups should be treated as a model diagnostic requiring interpretation and, where appropriate, sensitivity analysis. They are not evidence that Age has a causal effect on default.


The age-group table is a **limited subgroup diagnostic**, not a formal fairness determination. Age is strongly associated with the model score in these data, so differences in observed risk, calibration, recall, specificity, and flagging are reported transparently. A complete fairness audit would require a clear legal and decision context, additional protected-group variables, appropriate fairness definitions, and analysis of the consequences of the decision rule.


## Separate Validation / Stress Test

```{r separate-validation, results='asis'}
if (file.exists(params$validation_path)) {

  validation_data <- read.csv(
    params$validation_path,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  if (all(c(base_features, "Default") %in% names(validation_data))) {

    val_new_raw <- prepare_inputs(validation_data)

    val_new_baked <- as.data.frame(
      recipes::bake(
        rec,
        new_data = val_new_raw
      )
    )

    p_new <- predict_selected(val_new_baked)
    y_new <- as.integer(validation_data$Default)

    new_prob <- probability_metrics(y_new, p_new)
    new_class <- class_metrics(
      y_new,
      p_new,
      selected_threshold
    )

    new_summary <- cbind(
      N = length(y_new),
      DefaultRate = mean(y_new),
      new_prob,
      new_class
    )

    new_display <- new_summary |>
      mutate(
        across(
          where(is.numeric),
          ~ round(.x, 4)
        )
      )

    cat("\n\n")
    print(
      paper_kable(
        new_display |>
          select(
            N, DefaultRate, LogLoss,
            Brier, ROC_AUC, PR_AUC
          ),
        caption = "Probability performance on the separate stress-test data."
      )
    )

    cat("\n\n")
    print(
      paper_kable(
        new_display |>
          select(
            Threshold, Recall, Precision,
            Specificity, FalsePositiveRate,
            FlaggedRate, Accuracy
          ),
        caption = "Operating characteristics on the separate stress-test data."
      )
    )

    cat(
      "\n\nThe additional validation file is used as a stress test. ",
      "Its synthetic construction means that it does not constitute independent external validation. ",
      "It is included to examine how the fixed model behaves under a deliberately shifted population.\n\n"
    )

  } else {
    cat(
      "The separate validation file exists but does not contain the full required predictor set and Default label."
    )
  }

} else {
  cat(
    "No separate validation file was found. The analysis therefore reports internal held-out validation and testing only."
  )
}
```



## Predictive Stability Under Controlled Distribution Shift

The empirical results above establish the internally validated baseline. The following results examine what happens to the same statistical properties when the deployment distribution is deliberately changed.

### Covariate shift under correct specification

Under the correctly specified logistic model, raw log loss increases as \(\delta\) increases, but the oracle loss increases almost identically because the event distribution and composition of the deployment population also change.

```{r shift-correct-spec-table}
shift_correct <- data.frame(
  delta = c(0,0.5,1,1.5,2),
  event_rate = c(.1201204,.1623476,.2141752,.2758440,.3461644),
  model_log_loss = c(.3169038,.3811773,.4444422,.5025753,.5498226),
  oracle_log_loss = c(.3164975,.3805876,.4436485,.5015168,.5483225),
  excess_log_loss = c(.0004063,.0005897,.0007937,.0010585,.0015001),
  model_brier = c(.09337461,.11753734,.14235274,.16590170,.18554562),
  oracle_brier = c(.09326659,.11734461,.14205723,.16548040,.18491982),
  probability_mse = c(.0001154,.0001827,.0002856,.0004310,.0006202)
)
paper_kable(shift_correct, digits=4,
             caption="Pure covariate shift under correct model specification.")
```

Probability MSE remains small, increasing from approximately 0.00012 to 0.00062. The fitted model therefore remains close to the oracle even as the population changes substantially. This control condition shows that raw predictive loss should not be interpreted without considering the changing deployment problem itself.

### Covariate shift exposes model misspecification

When the true outcome mechanism contains an omitted quadratic term, the effect of covariate shift changes substantially.

```{r shift-misspec-table}
shift_misspec <- data.frame(
  beta4=rep(c(0,.25,.50),each=5),
  delta=rep(c(0,.5,1,1.5,2),3),
  event_rate=c(
    .1199140,.1622352,.2138992,.2758176,.3455884,
    .1203524,.1778836,.2634096,.3756868,.5063260,
    .1200520,.1881532,.2954800,.4349040,.5908256),
  probability_mse=c(
    .0001101,.0001735,.0002743,.0004222,.0006156,
    .0011548,.0025585,.0058773,.0118930,.0206164,
    .0043014,.0079675,.0163664,.0293055,.0442197),
  excess_log_loss=c(
    .0004141,.0005302,.0007506,.0010641,.0015018,
    .0052946,.0072391,.0146766,.0301216,.0539815,
    .0220819,.0239697,.0435808,.0778375,.1224249),
  excess_brier=c(
    .0001123,.0001690,.0002790,.0004234,.0006289,
    .0011949,.0025778,.0058386,.0119148,.0205772,
    .0043277,.0079292,.0164331,.0292433,.0441432)
)
paper_kable(shift_misspec, digits=4,
             caption="Probability deterioration under covariate shift and model misspecification.")
```

At \(\delta=2\), probability MSE is approximately 0.00062 under correct specification but approximately 0.04422 under strong misspecification. The shift therefore magnifies an approximation error that is much smaller near the development population.

The calibration and discrimination results reveal a second feature.

```{r shift-calibration-discrimination-table}
shift_caldisc <- data.frame(
 beta4=rep(c(0,.25,.50),each=5),
 delta=rep(c(0,.5,1,1.5,2),3),
 model_auc=c(.7624,.7597,.7579,.7556,.7537,
             .7829,.8077,.8228,.8339,.8437,
             .7873,.8420,.8651,.8771,.8883),
 oracle_auc=c(.7629,.7602,.7584,.7561,.7541,
              .7892,.8116,.8278,.8413,.8540,
              .8174,.8530,.8753,.8904,.9044),
 cal_intercept=c(.0043,.0045,.0091,.0104,.0094,
                 .0077,.2285,.4101,.5682,.7188,
                 -.0077,.4661,.7711,1.0009,1.2132),
 cal_slope=c(1.0014,.9992,1.0021,1.0022,.9999,
             1.0044,1.1495,1.2682,1.3695,1.4559,
             .9918,1.3171,1.5401,1.6905,1.8097),
 probability_mse=c(.0001153,.0001825,.0002852,.0004305,.0006193,
                   .0011231,.0025356,.0057941,.0118162,.0204316,
                   .0042941,.0079142,.0162069,.0291789,.0439657)
)
paper_kable(shift_caldisc, digits=4,
             caption="Discrimination and calibration under covariate shift.")
```

Under strong misspecification, model ROC-AUC increases from approximately 0.787 to 0.888 as \(\delta\) moves from 0 to 2, while probability MSE increases from approximately 0.0043 to 0.0440 and the calibration slope increases from approximately 0.99 to 1.81. The deployment population becomes easier to rank while the numerical probabilities become less accurate.

### Decision-threshold stability

The optimal balanced-accuracy threshold moves systematically with the deployment population.

```{r shift-threshold-data}
shift_threshold <- data.frame(
 beta4=rep(c(0,.25,.50),each=5),
 delta=rep(c(0,.5,1,1.5,2),3),
 baseline_threshold=c(rep(.1222,5),rep(.1374,5),rep(.1600,5)),
 shifted_threshold=c(.1232,.1640,.2156,.2752,.3468,
                     .1379,.1927,.2585,.3264,.3948,
                     .1605,.2142,.2741,.3329,.3954),
 threshold_change=c(.00091,.04176,.09335,.15290,.22456,
                    .00045,.05525,.12110,.18903,.25741,
                    .00054,.05423,.11419,.17291,.23540),
 frozen_BA=c(.6912,.6808,.6518,.6159,.5794,
             .7112,.7187,.6949,.6549,.6130,
             .7285,.7558,.7379,.6993,.6560),
 adapted_BA=c(.6911,.6911,.6879,.6866,.6850,
              .7111,.7325,.7446,.7527,.7610,
              .7284,.7675,.7843,.7930,.8033),
 BA_gain=c(-.00018,.01026,.03603,.07068,.10554,
           -.00006,.01374,.04969,.09777,.14795,
           -.00013,.01177,.04644,.09377,.14724),
 mcse_threshold_change=c(.0009970,.0010493,.0011887,.0013209,.0015066,
                         .0010914,.0011807,.0012064,.0013443,.0014906,
                         .0011857,.0011820,.0011874,.0013004,.0014879),

)

threshold_plot_data <- shift_threshold |>
 dplyr::mutate(
   condition=factor(beta4, levels=c(0,.25,.50),
   labels=c("Correct specification","Moderate misspecification","Strong misspecification"))
 )

ggplot(threshold_plot_data,
       aes(x=delta,y=shifted_threshold,linetype=condition,shape=condition))+

   title="Optimal Decision Thresholds Under Covariate Shift",

 )+

```

```{r shift-threshold-table}
threshold_display <- shift_threshold |>
  transmute(
    `beta4` = beta4,
    `delta` = delta,
    `Baseline threshold` = baseline_threshold,
    `Shifted threshold` = shifted_threshold,
    `Threshold change` = threshold_change,

  digits = 4,

)
```

Even under correct specification, the mean optimal threshold rises from approximately 0.122 at baseline to 0.347 at \(\delta=2\). Under strong misspecification, the threshold rises from approximately 0.160 to 0.395. At \(\delta=2\), the frozen threshold produces mean balanced accuracy of approximately 0.656 compared with approximately 0.803 after threshold adaptation, a gain of approximately 0.147 with MCSE approximately 0.00114.

### Intercept outcome shift: calibration can fail while ranking remains stable

```{r shift-intercept-data}
shift_intercept <- data.frame(
 gamma=c(0,.25,.50,.75,1),
 event_rate=c(.119813,.145332,.173938,.206933,.242880),
 model_auc=c(.762216,.760635,.758814,.757014,.756428),
 oracle_auc=c(.762693,.761109,.759335,.757490,.756924),
 auc_gap=c(.0004777,.0004740,.0005212,.0004760,.0004969),
 cal_intercept=c(.001893,.259570,.503086,.753589,1.005151),
 mcse_cal_intercept=c(.0057779,.0056823,.0058504,.0056817,.0055904),
 cal_slope=c(1.00153,1.00297,1.00066,1.00037,1.00276),
 mcse_cal_slope=c(.0031230,.0030244,.0029529,.0028854,.0029063),
 probability_mse=c(.0001099,.0010454,.0042315,.0103535,.0200985),
 excess_log_loss=c(.0004138,.0038023,.0148087,.0356018,.0674526)
)

intercept_plot <- rbind(
 data.frame(gamma=shift_intercept$gamma,parameter="Calibration intercept",
            estimate=shift_intercept$cal_intercept,theory=shift_intercept$gamma),
 data.frame(gamma=shift_intercept$gamma,parameter="Calibration slope",
            estimate=shift_intercept$cal_slope,theory=1)
)

ggplot(intercept_plot,aes(x=gamma,y=estimate))+
 geom_line(linewidth=.8)+geom_point(size=2.7)+
 geom_line(aes(y=theory),linetype="dashed",linewidth=.6)+
 facet_wrap(~parameter,scales="free_y")+
 labs(
   title="Calibration Under Intercept Outcome Shift",
   subtitle="Simulation estimates closely follow the theoretical relationship",
   x=expression(paste("Intercept shift (",gamma,")")),
   y="Calibration parameter"
 )+

```

```{r shift-intercept-table}
intercept_display_a <- shift_intercept |>
  transmute(
    `Intercept shift (gamma)` = gamma,
    `Event rate` = event_rate,
    `Model AUC` = model_auc,
    `Oracle AUC` = oracle_auc,
    `AUC gap` = auc_gap
  )

intercept_display_b <- shift_intercept |>
  transmute(
    `Intercept shift (gamma)` = gamma,
    `Calibration intercept` = cal_intercept,
    `MCSE: intercept` = mcse_cal_intercept,
    `Calibration slope` = cal_slope,
    `MCSE: slope` = mcse_cal_slope,
    `Probability MSE` = probability_mse,
    `Excess log loss` = excess_log_loss
  )

paper_kable(
  intercept_display_a,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Intercept outcome shift: event rate and discrimination."
)

paper_kable(
  intercept_display_b,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Intercept outcome shift: calibration and probability accuracy."
)
```

The calibration intercept closely tracks the imposed value of \(\gamma\), while the calibration slope remains approximately one. At \(\gamma=1\), the mean calibration intercept is approximately 1.005 and the mean slope is approximately 1.003. Probability MSE rises from approximately 0.00011 to 0.02010, yet the model--oracle AUC gap remains about 0.0005. The model therefore retains ranking information while its absolute probabilities become systematically wrong.

    `Event rate` = event_rate,
