```{r shift-slope-table}
  caption = "Slope outcome shift: calibration and probability accuracy."
)
```

With event prevalence held near 12%, the original model's ROC-AUC falls from approximately 0.762 to 0.473 as the true effect of \(X_1\) weakens and reverses. At the strongest shift, the oracle ROC-AUC is approximately 0.764, producing an AUC gap of approximately 0.291 with MCSE approximately 0.00093. The calibration slope falls from approximately 1.00 to \(-0.09\), probability MSE increases to approximately 0.02672, and excess log loss reaches approximately 0.11914.

The oracle remains informative because the prediction problem itself still contains signal; the original model fails because the relationship it learned is no longer the deployment relationship.

### Integrated result

The experiments do not produce one universal pattern of model deterioration. Covariate shift can expose misspecification and alter operating thresholds; intercept outcome shift can damage calibration while preserving ranking; and slope outcome shift can damage both calibration and discrimination. The common implication is that stable or improving ROC-AUC does not guarantee stable probabilities, calibration, or decision rules.


\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Discussion

This study began with a practical loan-default prediction problem but leads to a broader statistical conclusion about predictive inference under distributional change. The empirical analysis establishes a model that performs reasonably well under internal validation. The simulation analysis then shows why that evidence should not be interpreted as proof that the same probabilities, calibration, ranking, or decision threshold will remain appropriate after deployment.

The empirical model-selection exercise is therefore a supporting component rather than the final research question. Raw logistic regression achieved the lowest validation log loss among the candidate models, with performance very close to Platt-calibrated logistic regression. The more flexible random-forest and boosting candidates did not improve probability estimation under the prespecified validation criterion in this dataset. On the locked test set, the selected model achieved ROC-AUC 0.7585, PR-AUC 0.3288, Brier score 0.0908, and log loss 0.3111. Its calibration intercept and slope were close to the ideal values, providing evidence that the probability scale was appropriate for the held-out observations drawn from the same source.

The threshold analysis adds a separate decision layer. Balanced accuracy selected a validation threshold of 0.1175, which produced test recall of approximately 0.684 and specificity of approximately 0.701. This threshold is not an intrinsic property of logistic regression and is not an economically optimal lending cutoff. It is the solution to a particular statistical operating objective under the validation population.

The covariate-shift experiments explain why internal success may not transfer unchanged to deployment. When the conditional logistic model was correctly specified, moving the distribution of \(X_1\) produced only small excess probability error relative to the oracle. This is an important control result: a change in \(P(X)\) does not automatically invalidate a correct model of \(P(Y\mid X)\). Raw loss can increase simply because the composition and event distribution of the population have changed.

The result changes when the fitted model is misspecified. Omitting a quadratic effect creates an approximation error that is relatively modest near the development distribution but becomes much larger as deployment moves toward regions where the omitted curvature matters more. This demonstrates an interaction between covariate shift and model misspecification rather than a universal failure of logistic regression under shift.

The same experiment also demonstrates why discrimination should not be treated as a complete measure of predictive validity. Under strong misspecification, ROC-AUC increased as covariate shift became stronger even though probability MSE and calibration error deteriorated substantially. The deployment population became easier to rank, but the numerical probabilities became less trustworthy. AUC therefore answered the ranking question correctly while failing to reveal a different probability-estimation problem.

The intercept-shift experiment isolates that distinction further. The estimated calibration intercept closely followed the imposed shift, the calibration slope remained near one, and the model--oracle AUC gap remained negligible. The old model continued to rank observations effectively but systematically underestimated the new level of risk. In a setting approximating this structure, recalibration may be sufficient because the ordering information has largely survived.

The slope-shift experiment represents a fundamentally different failure. When the true effect of \(X_1\) weakened and eventually reversed, the original model's ranking deteriorated even though the oracle remained informative. At the strongest shift, the original ROC-AUC fell below 0.50 while the oracle remained near 0.764. This is not a problem that an intercept correction alone can solve because the predictor--outcome relationship itself has changed.

Decision-threshold stability provides a final distinction. Even under correct model specification, the balanced-accuracy-optimal threshold moved substantially after covariate shift. Thus model validity and decision-rule validity are not identical. A model may still estimate useful conditional probabilities while the operating threshold chosen for the development population becomes suboptimal for a new deployment population.

These results change how the empirical loan model should be interpreted. The test-set results establish internal predictive performance under the observed data source. They do not establish that a future borrower population will have the same predictor distribution, baseline default risk, conditional predictor effects, calibration, or optimal review threshold. The simulation does not prove that these shifts occur in the empirical data; rather, it identifies the statistical consequences that would follow if different forms of shift occurred.

For deployment monitoring, the findings argue against relying on ROC-AUC alone. A probability-based risk system should separately monitor input distributions, event prevalence, calibration intercept and slope, probability losses such as Brier score or log loss once outcomes mature, ranking measures, score distributions, review rates, and threshold operating characteristics. The appropriate intervention depends on the observed failure mode. Intercept recalibration, broader recalibration, threshold revision, and complete model redevelopment are statistically different responses to different problems.

The central result can therefore be stated compactly:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Stable discrimination does not guarantee stable probabilities, calibration, or decisions under distribution shift.}
}
\]

That conclusion is broader than the specific loan dataset. It concerns the deployment of probability models whenever the future population may differ from the population used for development.

\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Limitations

Several limitations constrain interpretation of the empirical and simulation evidence.

First, the empirical `Default` response has no documented observation horizon. The fitted probabilities therefore concern the recorded default outcome rather than a verified 12-month, lifetime, or regulatory probability of default.

Second, the empirical data contain no loan-origination or outcome dates. The train/calibration/validation/test design is stratified rather than chronological, so the study cannot establish performance on a genuinely later origination cohort.

Third, the data do not contain a borrower identifier that establishes whether the same borrower can appear more than once. The analysis therefore assumes independent loan records. If repeated borrowers exist, borrower-grouped splitting would be necessary.

Fourth, the dataset contains no longitudinal repayment history, days-past-due trajectory, recoveries, exposure at default, or loss given default. The empirical model is therefore a binary recorded-default risk model rather than a time-to-default, early-warning, or expected-loss model.

Fifth, the separate validation file is synthetic and functions only as a stress test. It does not constitute genuine external validation and cannot establish transportability to an independent lending population.

Sixth, balanced accuracy is a statistical threshold objective. The available data do not contain verified costs of false negatives and false positives, review-capacity constraints, revenues, recoveries, EAD, or LGD required to establish an economically optimal threshold.

Seventh, the subgroup analysis is descriptive and incomplete. The available variables do not support a comprehensive fairness audit, and the study does not make a fairness determination.

The simulation study is deliberately stylized. It uses three independent normally distributed predictors and logistic data-generating mechanisms so that specific forms of shift can be isolated. Real lending populations may contain correlated predictors, interactions, missingness, policy effects, temporal dependence, and several simultaneous forms of distribution change.

The simulated values of \(\delta\), \(\beta_4\), \(\gamma\), and \(\kappa\) are experimental design conditions, not empirical estimates of real credit-market drift. The simulation establishes mechanisms under controlled assumptions; it does not establish that any particular shift occurred in the observed loan dataset.

Finally, the Monte Carlo standard errors quantify simulation precision, not uncertainty about real-world future performance. Genuine claims about deployment transportability require temporal or external data.

\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Future Research

The most important next step is empirical validation under real distributional change. A dataset with documented origination dates, outcome dates, a defined default horizon, and later-period cohorts would permit direct out-of-time evaluation of calibration, discrimination, and threshold stability. Data from an independent lender or lending environment would provide an even stronger transportability test.

A second extension is adaptation after detected shift. The present study characterizes several failure modes; future work should compare intercept-only recalibration, recalibration of both intercept and slope, threshold revision, importance weighting under covariate shift, and complete model refitting. Each adaptation method should be estimated on a dedicated adaptation sample and evaluated on a separate shifted holdout sample.

A richer credit-risk application should incorporate longitudinal repayment histories, exposure at default, loss given default, recoveries, review costs, and revenues. Those quantities would allow the operating rule to be chosen using expected loss or utility rather than balanced accuracy.

Finally, the simulation framework can be extended across sample size, baseline prevalence, signal strength, correlated predictors, alternative nonlinearities, interactions, and simultaneous changes in \(P(X)\) and \(P(Y\mid X)\). Such work would move from illustrating distinct failure mechanisms toward identifying conditions under which particular adaptation strategies are statistically reliable.

\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Reproducibility and Software

The empirical workflow is implemented in R Markdown with a fixed development design, training-only preprocessing, saved model objects, and a validation-selected threshold. The associated Shiny application uses the same saved probability model, preprocessing recipe, calibration choice, and threshold, and is intended as a research and decision-support interface rather than an automated lending-decision system.

The distribution-shift experiments use 500 Monte Carlo replications per condition with simulation seed 1998. The manuscript records the frozen simulation summaries and reconstructs the reported tables and figures from those results. Monte Carlo standard errors are reported where they are central to the interpretation.

Code is hidden in the rendered manuscript so that the PDF emphasizes the statistical design, results, and interpretation while the R Markdown source preserves the computational workflow.

\FloatBarrier
\clearpage

# Conclusion

This study evaluates loan-default prediction as a probability-based system that must remain statistically meaningful beyond the development sample. The empirical analysis establishes the internal baseline: raw logistic regression achieved the lowest validation log loss among the candidate models, produced useful held-out discrimination, remained close to ideal calibration, and supported a validation-selected balanced-accuracy threshold of 0.1175.

The central contribution comes from asking what happens to those same properties when the deployment distribution changes. Pure covariate shift produced little excess probability error when the conditional model was correctly specified, but the combination of covariate shift and model misspecification produced substantial calibration and probability deterioration. Intercept outcome shift altered absolute risk while largely preserving ranking. Slope outcome shift changed the predictor--outcome relationship itself and eventually destroyed the original model's discrimination. The operating threshold also moved substantially across deployment populations, including under correct specification.

The broader conclusion is that **distribution shift does not create one universal form of predictive failure**. Different changes in the data-generating process affect different parts of the predictive system. A model can retain or improve discrimination while its probabilities become miscalibrated, remain probabilistically useful while its decision threshold becomes inappropriate, or lose ranking ability when predictor effects change.

Accordingly, internal test performance should be treated as evidence about the development environment rather than as proof of future stability. Probability accuracy, calibration, discrimination, and decision performance should be evaluated and monitored as distinct but connected properties of a deployed predictive model.
